newsitem.title: CHINA: China says all Taiwan-HK contact needs approval.
newsitem.headline: China says all Taiwan-HK contact needs approval.

text.p: Beijing said on Thursday any official contact or exchanges between rival Taiwan and China's new territory of Hong Kong needed the approval of the central government.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman was speaking shortly after a meeting in Hong Kong between the enclave's chief executive Tung Chee-hwa and Taiwan's top negotiator with China Koo Chen-fu.

He was answering questions from foreign reporters on Beijing's response to the first high-level contact between Taiwan and Hong Kong since the former British colony reverted to Beijing rule on Tuesday.

"Official contact, exchanges, negotiations, signing of agreements and the establishment of offices between the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and the Taiwan region must be reported to the central government for approval," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang said.

There was no suggestion that Tung had not received Beijing's prior approval for the meeting with Koo, head of Taipei's Straits Exchange Foundation. It came just a day after Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen left Hong Kong following a string of triumphal handover ceremonies.
The foundation is an intermediary body that Taiwan has authorised to handle contacts with communist China in the absence of formal relations between the two sides.
A host of issues need to be ironed out in the economically crucial Hong Kong-Taiwan relationship that has become even more sensitive politically since the handover.
Much of Taiwan's massive trade and investment in the Chinese mainland passes through Hong Kong because of Taipei's ban on direct exchanges with the mainland.
The ban dates from 1949, when the Chinese Nationalist government fled to the island after losing a civil war with the communists. Beijing considers Taiwan a renegade province.

Taiwan has enormous commercial interests in Hong Kong and on the mainland. The former British colony, a major world banking centre, has been a crucial funnel for Taiwan investment to the mainland over the past decade.
Tung's family business, the Orient Overseas (International) Ltd also has substantial dealings with Taiwan companies.

An aide to Tung played down the meeting, saying it would be informal, but analysts noted that it came soon after Tung had predicted fast progress in sorting out Hong Kong's post-handover relationship with Taiwan.
China's Tang said relations between Hong Kong and Taiwan should respect the one-China principle and should not create "two Chinas", "one China, one Taiwan" or Taiwan independence.
"Two Chinas" and "one China, one Taiwan" are phrases Beijing employs to refer to its concerns that Taiwan may abandon its official goal of reunification with China and declare independence.
China has threatened to invade if Taiwan declared independence. Taiwan has denied any dreams of independence and says it is committed to reunification under a democratic system.
The Beijing spokesman said the "one country, two systems" formula was workable in Hong Kong and Macau and was also workable in Taiwan.
Portuguese-run Macau, across the Pearl River estuary from Hong Kong, is due to return to Chinese rule in December 1999.
Taiwan has rejected the "one country, two systems" formula devised by the late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Under the formula, Beijing has promised to allow Hong Kong to keep its capitalist lifestyle for 50 years after the transfer to Chinese sovereignty.
Reunification between China and Taiwan would be realised regardless of any difficulties, Tang said.
He shrugged off protests this week by democrats in Hong Kong against the inauguration of a new Beijing-anointed legislature, saying "unharmonious sounds... do not win the people's hearts".
